extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, calculus/transition-to-proof instructors, and survey instrument designers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for (1) assessing student understanding of mathematical concepts (especially equivalence relations: concept image, definition, and usage) via task-based interviews and classroom interventions; and (2) designing/validating multi-instrument surveys to identify characteristics of successful Calculus I programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept-understanding scheme (definition, image, usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concept-understanding scheme: concept definition, concept image, and concept usage as distinct dimensions of student understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concept definition = formal definition; concept image = the mental picture evoked by examples, diagrams, etc.; concept usage = how the student operates with the concept in generating examples or writing proofs. Assess all three to capture students' understanding (Moore, 1994).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An equivalence relation must be reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess students' ability to recall and correctly state each requirement symbolically and to recognize/failures of these properties in examples. Note common student errors involve misuse of quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing concept image
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate students' informal/evoked images and related concepts (e.g., partitions, prototypical examples) when asked 'what is an equivalence relation?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe what other concepts, ideas, or illustrations come to mind; count connections to partitions or concrete prototypes (e.g., sorting colored shapes) as indicators of a richer concept image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing concept definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate students' recall and formulation of the formal (symbolic/verbal) definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask students to describe each requirement formally and attend to correct use of quantifiers; compare written definitions across instructional conditions to detect differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing concept usage (proof-writing and example generation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess students by asking them to determine whether given relations are equivalence relations and to prove or disprove those claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require students to produce examples of related and non-related elements to ensure understanding of notation; ask them to 'talk out loud' and prompt for clarification when reasoning is unclear; categorize their proof schemes (empirical vs deductive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-scheme classification (empirical vs deductive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize students' arguments as empirical (example-based) or deductive (definition-based).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to evaluate concept usage quality; higher rates of deductive arguments indicate stronger formal/definition-based reasoning. Report proportions (e.g., 4/17 vs 14/21) as outcome measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to partitions as an evaluative indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether students make the conceptual link between equivalence relations and partitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count mentions or demonstrations connecting equivalence classes to partitions; stronger linkage indicates more interconnected concept image and better conceptual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional comparison metric: small-group activities vs lecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare instructional formats by their effects on concept image, concept usage, and proof success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key outcome measures include number of students who mention partitions, number producing correct formal proofs, and tendency to use deductive reasoning. Use task-based interviews several weeks after instruction to assess lasting effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional design principle: example generation and exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: Design activities to help students develop informal understanding through example generation, reformulation, decomposition/synthesis, and avoidance of pure memorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete manipulatives (colored shapes), have students classify relations (e.g., 'same color' vs 'differ in exactly one attribute'), ask them to produce examples/non-examples, and encourage group discussion to build prototypical examples that embody formal definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment interview protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Task-based interviews procedure for assessing understanding: initial open question, probes for related concepts, tasks to judge relations, request for examples/non-examples, talk-aloud, and researcher prompts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews should be videotaped, last ~30 minutes, ensure notation is understood by asking for examples, and use probes to clarify reasoning. Repeat probing can reveal gained concepts; conduct follow-up probes to reveal depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common student difficulties to note
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical student problems: misuse of quantifiers, reliance on informal/empirical arguments, weak linkage between formal definition and partition concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these observed error patterns to inform instruction and to interpret assessment data; design probes specifically targeting quantifier comprehension and definition-based reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of survey dependent variables (student post-survey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Student post-survey dependent variables include: A) Course grade and intention to take Calc II (with 4 subcategories), B) Impact of Calc I course on student (with 4 subcategories), and C) Student self-perception of knowledge/skills in calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the primary outcomes the survey seeks to measure; each dimension may be broken into multiple subcategories in the full taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of survey independent variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential independent variables: A) Student Beliefs and Affect (5 subcategories), B) Perceived Behaviors and Values of the Calculus Instructor (4 subcategories), C) The Role of Homework and Exams (4 subcategories), D) The Role and Behavior of the Student in Learning (6 subcategories), E) Supports for Students (2 subcategories), F) Readiness for Calculus (Pre-survey) (3 subcategories), G) Readiness for Calculus (Post-survey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These independent variables are hypothesized (from literature) to influence the dependent outcomes and should be operationalized into survey items aligned with the taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for selecting survey variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Select variables based on (1) strength of evidence in literature, (2) amenability to change/manipulation by instructor or department, (3) respondent burden (how hard to answer), and (4) expected reliability (likelihood respondents answer truthfully).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance comprehensiveness with feasibility; exclude variables that are weak predictors, not amenable to intervention, overly burdensome, or unlikely to yield reliable responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey question format selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose question formats (Likert, contrasting alternative, categorical, matrix) depending on the information sought and measurement properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasting alternative formats when Likert scales are ambiguous; provide brief descriptions for each end of the scale to clarify meaning. Example provided: a contrasting alternative item asking whether an exam score measures understanding vs conformity to teacher's methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey development and validation process
rubrics_metrics.description: Iterative instrument development: construct items mapped to taxonomy variables, conduct clinical (talk-aloud) interviews with representative respondents, refine items and answer choices based on interview data, repeat until items assess intended variables and are interpreted consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include multiple cycles of item construction and cognitive interviewing for each survey (chair, coordinator, instructor pre/post, student pre/post). Seek external professional review (e.g., survey design experts) and pilot large-scale administration to check functioning (e.g., >10,000 pre-course respondents were obtained).

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey formatting and reliability considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider format choices to maximize validity and reliability for each taxonomy variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For constructs where relative endorsement of two alternatives is most informative, use contrasting alternatives with explicit end-point descriptions. Consult survey methodology literature (Colton & Covert; Fowler; Saris & Gallhofer) and domain experts during design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance/foci to measure in calculus program studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure departmental/instructional factors linked to persistence: sense of community/identity, institutional supports, instructional behaviors meeting intellectual needs, quality of interactive engagement, intellectual demand of homework and classroom tasks, student self-efficacy and identity with mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constructs inform the selection of survey variables and interpretation of results; pay attention to differential effects across demographic groups (race/ethnicity, gender).
